summary.text: The Medieval Warm Period was a spell of warm climate in the North Atlantic region lasting from about 950 to about 1250 CE.
Peak warmth arrived at different times in different regions, so it was not one uniform worldwide event.
Possible causes include stronger solar activity, fewer volcanic eruptions and shifts in ocean circulation, and a cooler period called the Little Ice Age followed it.

items.prompt: Records from one region show peak medieval warmth around 1000 CE, while another region's peak comes a century later. What does this suggest?

options.label: One of the two records must simply be wrong
The warmth was regional rather than worldwide
The whole planet warmed in perfect step
Climate records cannot show past warmth

items.explain: Peak warmth came at different times in different regions, which shows the period was not a globally uniform event.

items.prompt: Norse settlers in Greenland first kept cattle, sheep and goats. After the climate turned colder and stormier around 1250, what happened to their diet?

options.label: They switched to growing wheat and barley
They lived on grain shipped from Europe
It shifted toward food from the ocean
It stayed much the same as before

items.explain: Their diet steadily shifted toward ocean sources, and by around 1300 seal hunting supplied over three quarters of their food.

items.prompt: Some scientists prefer to call this era the 'Medieval Climatic Anomaly'. What point does that name make?

options.label: Climate changes other than warmth mattered too
The era was mostly colder than the present
The warmth lasted for only a single decade
The era actually fell outside medieval times

items.explain: The name is used to stress that climatic effects other than temperature were also important.

items.prompt: The last Europeans left Greenland gradually over the decades after 1412. What mainly drove them away?

options.label: A single raid that wiped out the settlements
A volcanic eruption that buried their farms
A plague that killed nearly everyone at once
Economics, such as more farms free in Scandinavia

items.explain: The gradual withdrawal seems to have been caused mainly by economic factors, such as more farms becoming available in Scandinavian countries.

items.prompt: Climate models show that natural ups and downs alone cannot explain the medieval warmth. What does that point to?

options.label: Smoke from medieval industry warmed the air
An outside push, such as a brighter Sun, played a part
The warmth never really happened at all
Ocean currents on their own explain it fully

items.explain: Modelling shows an external forcing had to be one of the causes; increased solar activity and fewer volcanic eruptions are among the candidates.

items.prompt: During the medieval warmth, several smaller glaciers in southern Europe melted away completely. What became of the larger ones?

options.label: They survived and now hold clues to past climate
They vanished too, leaving no record behind
They doubled in size from the extra meltwater
They slid downhill and blocked the main rivers

items.explain: Larger glaciers in the region survived, and they now provide insight into the region's climate history.

paragraphs.heading: Three centuries of warmth
paragraphs.text: The Medieval Warm Period was a spell of warm climate around the North Atlantic, lasting from about 950 CE to about 1250 CE. It also goes by the Medieval Climate Optimum and the Medieval Climatic Anomaly. People who use that last name want to stress that changes other than temperature mattered too. Afterward came a cooler time, sometimes named the Little Ice Age, felt across the North Atlantic and in other regions too.

paragraphs.heading: What might have caused it
paragraphs.text: Several causes have been proposed: more activity on the Sun, fewer volcanic eruptions, and changes in how the ocean circulates. Computer models show that the climate's own natural ups and downs could not produce the warm period by themselves. Some outside push on the climate, which scientists call an external forcing, must have played a part.

paragraphs.heading: Global or regional
paragraphs.text: Whether the warmth covered the whole world or only some regions has been argued over for a long time. In 2019 the Pages-2k consortium, working with a larger collection of climate records, confirmed that it did not happen everywhere at once. The warmest 51-year stretch within it arrived at different times in different regions. Other studies, correcting for the fact that more research comes from northern areas, find that global temperatures stayed fairly stable for 7,000 years before the industrial revolution, with no worldwide Medieval Warm Period or Little Ice Age.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from the Atlantic
paragraphs.text: Sediment cores from the floor of the Sargasso Sea, dated by radiocarbon in a 1996 study by Keigwin, show surface water about 1 °C warmer 1,000 years ago, during the warm period. The same record shows water about 1 °C cooler 400 years ago, during the Little Ice Age. Layers of sediment sampled in Puerto Rico, along the Gulf Coast, and on the eastern seaboard between Florida and New England point to a peak in North Atlantic tropical cyclones during the warm period, then a lull. That same research team, Mann and colleagues, found southern Greenland and parts of North America warmer than in 1961–1990, and some regions warmer even than in 1990–2010.

paragraphs.heading: The Norse in Greenland
paragraphs.text: Around 985, Vikings set up the Eastern and Western Settlements near the southern tip of Greenland, and around 1000 CE it was warm enough for them to reach Newfoundland and found a short-lived outpost. At first the settlers kept cattle, sheep and goats, and seafood made up about a quarter of what they ate. Once the climate turned colder and stormier around 1250, they ate more and more from the sea, and by about 1300 seals supplied over three quarters of their food. The last document from the settlements dates from 1412. The remaining Europeans then seem to have left gradually, mainly for economic reasons such as more farms becoming available in Scandinavia.

paragraphs.heading: Summers, winters and glaciers
paragraphs.text: In Central Europe, winters were cold almost without a break from 1000 AD to the late 19th century. Summers tell a different story: an almost unbroken 140-year run of warm seasons from 1170 to 1310, interrupted by a sharp cold snap from 1195 to 1197. Glaciers in southern Europe shrank a great deal during the warm period. Yet the Gorner glacier in Switzerland, the second largest in the Alps, grew during cool, wet summers from 1140 to 1151 and reached its furthest point in 1168.
